# Richard Stallman
Richard Stallman, born in New York City in 1953, is a pioneering computer scientist and the founder of the free software movement. A former physics graduate student at MIT, he became a hacker in the late 1970s and eventually resigned from his position in 1984 to dedicate himself full-time to the GNU Project. His primary goal is to create a complete, free operating system (GNU) and to promote the philosophy that software should be "free," meaning users have the freedom to run, study, modify, and redistribute the source code. To achieve this, he developed the General Public License (GPL), a "copyleft" legal mechanism that ensures any derivative works remain free, and created essential tools such as the GNU Emacs editor, GCC compiler, and GNU Make.
Stallman is a staunch advocate for user privacy and digital rights, actively opposing proprietary software, digital rights management (DRM), and software patents. He utilizes specific terminology, distinguishing between "free software" and "open source," and often uses the term "GNU/Linux" to emphasize the GNU project's role in the operating system. Beyond his technical contributions, he is known for his activism against surveillance, his refusal to use non-free hardware or software (such as cell phones or key cards), and his public criticism of corporate practices. In 2019, he resigned from the Free Software Foundation and MIT following controversies surrounding his comments on the Jeffrey Epstein scandal, though he later returned to the FSF board in 2021. He has received numerous accolades, including a MacArthur Fellowship and honorary doctorates from universities worldwide.
